title: Five Bright Planets to Spot in November
summary:
November is a great month for planet watching, in the evening, around midnight, or just before dawn. In the evening, Saturn is the planet of choice, visible well up in the southern sky during mid-to-late evening hours. Through a telescope, the southern side of its famous ring system is currently tilted about 6.5 degrees toward our line of sight.

Around the middle of the night, Mars and Jupiter come into view above the east-northeast horizon. Just before dawn, they are high in the southern sky near the Sickle of Leo the Lion. Watch Mars move toward Jupiter early in the month, pass it on November 16, and then sail away to the east for the rest of November.

Venus is the star of the predawn sky. On November 1, it rises 55 minutes before the sun. By November 5, viewers around 40 degrees north latitude can see it rise one hour and 25 minutes before the sun and shine 15 degrees above the horizon at sunrise. By the end of the month, it rises nearly three and a half hours before the sun. On the next-to-last day, it reaches magnitude -4.9, its greatest brightness. Early in the month, a telescope may show it as a hairline crescent only a few percent lit.

Mercury joins the morning show from midmonth. It reaches its greatest western elongation, 20 degrees from the sun, on November 20. From November 16 to 26, it rises more than 95 minutes before sunrise. A handy measuring tool is your own fist: a clenched fist held at arm's length covers roughly 10 degrees of sky.

Special moments include November 7, when a waning crescent moon, Venus, and the blue star Spica bunch together before sunrise, and November 26, when orange-yellow Mars passes the blue-white star Regulus.
why_it_matters: Planet watching needs no special trip, and November gives clear chances to see five different planets. Knowing when and where to look turns an ordinary night sky into a changing show.

background_read: The five planets in this guide can be spotted at different times of night during November: some in the evening, some around midnight and some just before dawn.
Where a planet appears depends on the time and on the viewer's position, and a telescope can reveal details such as Saturn's tilted rings or Venus shown as a thin crescent.
Bright stars such as Spica and Regulus act as signposts that help watchers find planets nearby.
Simple measures help too: a clenched fist held at arm's length covers roughly 10 degrees of sky.
